questions.stem:
A car moves in a straight line along a horizontal road with constant acceleration $2\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-2}$
The car is moving with speed $15\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}$ in the direction of the acceleration when it passes a signpost on the road.
The car is modelled as a particle.

parts.label: a
parts.text: (a) Use the model to find the speed of the car $4\,\mathrm{s}$ after passing the signpost. (2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) M1: $v=15+(2\times4)$
A1: $=23$ ($\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}$)
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1: Use of $v = u + at$ or any other complete method to form an equation in $v$ only. Condone sign errors. e.g. May find $s$ first: $s=(15\times4)+\frac{1}{2}\times2\times4^2=76$ then either: $76=4v-\frac{1}{2}\times2\times4^2$ or: $76=\frac{(15+v)}{2}\times4$ or: $v^2=15^2+2\times2\times76$
- N.B. If they use $v = u + at$ and have $15 = u + (2\times4)$, M1A0. M0 if they clearly use an incorrect suvat formula or $u = 0$
- A1: cao. Must be positive. A0 if they get 23 but go on and do something with it. i.e. not ISW. N.B. 23 with no working can score both marks.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Figure 1 below shows the horizontal forces acting on the car.
Given that
• the car has mass $800\,\mathrm{kg}$
• the driving force of the engine has magnitude $D$ newtons
• the resistance to the motion of the car has magnitude $400\,\mathrm{N}$
• the acceleration of the car is $2\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-2}$ in the direction of the driving force
(b) use the model to find the value of $D$. (2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) M1: $D-400=800\times2$
A1: $(D=)\ 2000$
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1: Use of $F = ma$ to form an equation in $D$ or a complete expression for $D$, with correct number of terms, condone sign errors and $g$ in the $ma$ term.
- A1: cao. N.B. 2000 with no working can score both marks.

questions.stem:
A small box $B$ of mass $2\,\mathrm{kg}$ is dragged in a straight line, along a rough horizontal plane, at a constant speed by a force of magnitude $5\,\mathrm{N}$.
The line of action of the force makes an angle $\alpha$ with the plane, where $\sin\alpha=\frac{3}{5}$, as shown in Figure 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: (a) Show that the magnitude of the normal reaction of the plane on the box is $16.6\,\mathrm{N}$. (3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) M1: Resolve vertically
A1: $(\uparrow)\ 5\sin\alpha+R=2g$ oe
A1*: $(R=)\ 19.6-3=16.6$ ($\mathrm{N}$)*
Official notes (completeness pass):
- N.B. Penalise the use of $g = 9.81$ ONCE (the first time it is used) for the whole question.
- M1: Form an equation in $R$ and $\alpha$ only, with correct number of terms, condone sign errors and sin/cos confusion, $\sin\alpha$ may or may not be substituted. N.B. $3 + R = 2g$ oe, with no evidence of resolving the 5 N, e.g. not using $\sin\alpha$, is M0.
- A1: Correct equation, $\sin\alpha$ may or may not be be substituted. A1*: Given answer correctly obtained, with at least one line of working.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
At the instant when $B$ is at the point $O$ on the plane, the force of magnitude $5\,\mathrm{N}$ is removed.
(b) Describe the motion of the box after the force of magnitude $5\,\mathrm{N}$ is removed. (1)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) B1: The box decelerates, slows down, loses speed or velocity, will come to a stop or rest, loses momentum
Official notes (completeness pass):
- B1: Any equivalent statement. B0 if any incorrect extras e.g. box is stationary or at rest, doesn't move, will stop moving.

parts.label: c
parts.text: (c) Find the magnitude of the normal reaction of the plane on the box after the force of magnitude $5\,\mathrm{N}$ is removed. (1)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) B1: $(S=)\ 19.6$ or $20$ ($\mathrm{N}$)
Official notes (completeness pass):
- B1: Accept $2g$ if $g$ is not substituted for. B0 if they use $g = 9.81$ unless they have already been penalised in part (a).

parts.label: d
parts.text:
Given that after the force of magnitude $5\,\mathrm{N}$ is removed
• the box is modelled as a particle
• air resistance is modelled as being negligible
• the coefficient of friction between the box and the plane is modelled as $0.2$
• the speed of the box as it passes through $O$ is $4\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}$
• the box comes to rest at the point $X$ on the plane
(d) use the model to find the length $OX$. (4)
parts.mark_scheme:
(d) M1: Equation of motion along the plane: $-F=2a$ or $F=2a$
B1: $F=0.2\times$ their $S$
M1: $0^2=4^2-2\times0.2g\times d$ or $0^2=4^2+2\times0.2g\times d$ or $4^2=0^2+2\times0.2g\times d$
A1: $(OX=)\ 4.1$ (m) or $4.08$ (m)
OR
M1: Work done against friction $=Fd$
B1: $F=0.2\times$ their $S$
M1: $0.2\times2g\times d=\frac{1}{2}\times2\times4^2$
A1: $(d=OX=)\ 4.1$ (m) or $4.08$ (m)
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1: Correct number of terms. Condone an extra $g$ in $ma$ term. M0 if 2 is missing. N.B. M0 if they use a vertical force for $F$ e.g. $2g$ or 16.6
- B1: Seen (e.g. on a diagram) or implied.
- M1: Complete method to form an equation in $d$ (= $OX$) only, condone sign errors, using their calculated acceleration from an attempt at using $F = ma$. M0 if clearly using $\mu$ (0.2) or $-\mu$ for $a$ without any calculation.. e.g. may find $t$ first: $0=4-0.2gt \Rightarrow t=\frac{20}{g}\ (=\frac{100}{49})$ then $d=4\times\frac{20}{g}-\frac{1}{2}\times0.2g\times\left(\frac{20}{g}\right)^2$ or $d=0-\frac{1}{2}\times(-0.2g)\times\left(\frac{20}{g}\right)^2$ or $0^2=4^2+2\times(-0.2g)\times d$
- A1: Either answer. A0 for $\frac{40}{g}$

parts.label: e
parts.text: (e) State one limitation of the model, apart from ignoring air resistance, that could affect your answer to part (d). (1)
parts.mark_scheme:
(e) B1: the box (it) has been modelled as a particle
the box (it) will have size or shape or dimensions
the coefficient of friction has been modelled as being constant
the coefficient of friction may not be exactly 0.2 or may vary
the friction may vary
Official notes (completeness pass):
- B0 : the ground may not be horizontal, an inaccurate value of $g$ has been used, has not considered wind, the angle may not be accurate, any reference to the particle having mass (or not having mass). Ignore any reference to air resistance.
- B1: Any equivalent statement which refers to the model. B0 if incorrect extras.

questions.stem:
[In this question, $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ are horizontal unit vectors due east and due north respectively.]
A particle $P$ of mass $0.5\,\mathrm{kg}$ moves with constant acceleration $(2\mathbf{i}-2.4\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-2}$ on a smooth horizontal plane under the action of a constant horizontal force $\mathbf{F}\,\mathrm{N}$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: (a) Find $\mathbf{F}$ in terms of $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$. (1)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) B1: $(\mathbf{F}=)\ (\mathbf{i}-1.2\mathbf{j})$
Official notes (completeness pass):
- Accept column vectors throughout apart from in the final answer for (a) and (d) which must be in terms of i and j, but only penalise ONCE for the whole question. N.B. For final answers to (a), (b) and (d) , penalise incorrect vector notation.
- B1: Must be in terms of $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$. Do not accept $0.5\times(2\mathbf{i}-2.4\mathbf{j})$. Do not need $\mathbf{F}=$

parts.label: b
parts.text:
At time $t=0$, $P$ is moving with velocity $(-7\mathbf{i}+7.8\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}$
(b) Find the velocity of $P$ at time $t=2$ seconds. (2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) M1: $\mathbf{v}=(-7\mathbf{i}+7.8\mathbf{j})+2(2\mathbf{i}-2.4\mathbf{j})$
A1: $=(-3\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j})$ ($\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}$)
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1: Use of $\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{a}t$ or any other complete method, e.g. integration, to find an unsimplified expression for $\mathbf{v}$ at $t = 2$, condone sign errors. N.B. If using integration, must have used $t = 0$, $\mathbf{v}=(-7\mathbf{i}+7.8\mathbf{j})$ to find the constant of integration and included it in their expression for $\mathbf{v}$ at $t = 2$.
- A1: cao. N.B. Ignore if they go on and find the speed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: (c) Find the direction of motion of $P$ at time $t=2$ seconds, giving your answer as a bearing in degrees. (3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) M1: Use trig to find an equation in a relevant angle
A1: e.g. $\tan\alpha=1$ or $-1$
or $\sin\alpha=\frac{3}{\sqrt{3^2+3^2}}$ or $\frac{-3}{\sqrt{3^2+3^2}}$
or $\cos\alpha=\frac{3}{\sqrt{3^2+3^2}}$ or $\frac{-3}{\sqrt{3^2+3^2}}$
A1: $315°$
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1: Use trig to find an equation in a relevant angle for their $\mathbf{v}$. A1: Correct equation.
- A1: Cao (with or without the degree sign), must come from a correct $\mathbf{v}$. N.B. $\pm45°, \pm135°, \pm225°, -315°$ with no working scores M1A1. $315°$ with no working scores all 3 marks.

parts.label: d
parts.text:
At time $t=0$, $P$ passes through the point $O$.
At time $t=5$ seconds, $P$ passes through the point $A$.
(d) Find $\overrightarrow{OA}$ in terms of $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$. (2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(d) M1: $\overrightarrow{OA}=5(-7\mathbf{i}+7.8\mathbf{j})+\frac{1}{2}(2\mathbf{i}-2.4\mathbf{j})\times5^2$
A1: $=(-10\mathbf{i}+9\mathbf{j})$ (m)
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1: Use of $\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{u}t+\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}t^2$ with $t = 5$ or any other complete method, e.g. integration of their $\mathbf{v}=f(t)$ and use of $t = 5$ , to find an unsimplified expression for $\overrightarrow{OA}$ (No need to show that $\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{0}$). M0 if they use $\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{0}$
- A1: Must be in terms of $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$. N.B. Ignore if they go on and find the length $OA$

questions.stem:
[In this question, position vectors are given relative to a fixed origin $O$.]
At time $t$ seconds, where $t>0$, the position vector of a particle $P$ is $\mathbf{r}$ metres where
$\mathbf{r}=4t^{\frac{3}{2}}\mathbf{i}-t^2\mathbf{j}$

parts.label: a
parts.text: (a) Find the position vector of $P$ at $t=4$ (1)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) B1: $\mathbf{r}=(32\mathbf{i}-16\mathbf{j})$
Official notes (completeness pass):
- N.B. Accept column vectors throughout apart from in the answer to (c).
- B1: cao. N.B. Must be using correct vector notation, including brackets if using column vectors.

parts.label: b
parts.text: (b) Find the exact distance of $P$ from $O$ at $t=4$ (2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) M1: Use Pythagoras: $\sqrt{32^2+16^2}$ oe for their $\mathbf{r}$
A1: $16\sqrt{5}$ (m)
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1: For an unsimplified expression, using their $\mathbf{r}$, with the square root. A1: Accept any surd equivalent isw. N.B. Must come from $\mathbf{r}=(32\mathbf{i}-16\mathbf{j})$

parts.label: c
parts.text: (c) Find an expression for the velocity of $P$ at time $t$ seconds, where $t>0$, giving your answer in terms of $t$, $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ (2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) M1: Differentiate $\mathbf{r}$ wrt $t$ to obtain $\mathbf{v}$
A1: $6t^{\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{i}-2t\mathbf{j}$ oe ($\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}$)
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1: Both powers of $t$ decreasing by 1 (but not just division by $t$). N.B. M0 if $\mathbf{i}$ and/or $\mathbf{j}$ are missing and never reappear. A1: Must be in terms of $t$, $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$

parts.label: d
parts.text:
At $t=T$, the acceleration of $P$ is in a direction that is perpendicular to the line with equation $y=\frac{1}{3}x$
(d) Find the value of $T$. (4)
parts.mark_scheme:
(d) M1: Differentiate their $\mathbf{v}$ wrt $t$ to obtain $\mathbf{a}$
A1: $3t^{-\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j}$
M1: $\frac{3T^{-\frac{1}{2}}}{-2}=-\frac{1}{3}$ must see $\frac{\text{i component of their }\mathbf{a}}{\text{j component of their }\mathbf{a}}=-\frac{1}{3}$ oe
A1: $(T=)\ \frac{81}{4}$ oe
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1: Both powers of $t$ decreasing by 1 (but not just division by $t$). If no i's and/or j's, can score M1 if EITHER they have 2 separate components, provided they are clearly treated as such in the subsequent working OR the i's and j's reappear otherwise M0.
- A1: Correct vector or 2 correct separate components, provided they are clearly treated as such in the subsequent working
- M1: Complete method to form a correct equation in $T$ ($t$) only, for their $\mathbf{a}$, using the 2 components from their $\mathbf{a}$. A1: Accept 20.3 or 20.25 or any equivalent fraction (allow $t$ instead of $T$)

parts.label: a

A1: $14\cos\theta\times t=40$

questions.stem:
A uniform rod $AB$ has mass $M$ and length $2a$.
A particle of mass $2M$ is attached to the rod at the point $C$, where $AC=0.5a$
The rod rests with end $A$ on rough horizontal ground and end $B$ against a vertical wall.
The rod lies in a vertical plane which is perpendicular to the wall.
The rod is in equilibrium at an angle $\alpha$ to the wall, as shown in Figure 4.
In an initial model
• the vertical wall is modelled as being smooth
• the magnitude of the normal reaction of the ground on the rod at $A$ is $R$
• the magnitude of the force exerted on the rod by the wall at $B$ is $S$
Using the model,

parts.label: a
parts.text: (a) find $R$ in terms of $M$ and $g$ (1)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) B1: $(\uparrow)$: $(R=)\ 3Mg$
Official notes (completeness pass):
- B1: Cao. Must be in terms of $M$ and $g$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: (b) show that $S=Mg\tan\alpha$ (3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) EITHER:
M1: Obtain an equation in $S$, $M$, $a$ and $\alpha$ only, by taking moments about $A$
A1: $\mathrm{M}(A)$: $S\times2a\cos\alpha=Mga\sin\alpha+2Mg\times0.5a\sin\alpha$
OR:
M1: Obtain an equation in $S$, $M$, $a$ and $\alpha$ only, by taking moments about $B$, $C$ or $G$ and resolving once and eliminating $F$ and $R$ (N.B. $R=3Mg$ from (a))
A1: Correct equation in $S$, $M$, $a$ and $\alpha$ only
Possible Moments equations:
$\mathrm{M}(B)$: $R\times2a\sin\alpha=Mga\sin\alpha+2Mg\times1.5a\sin\alpha+F\times2a\cos\alpha$
or $\mathrm{M}(C)$: $F\times0.5a\cos\alpha+S\times1.5a\cos\alpha=R\times0.5a\sin\alpha+Mg\times0.5a\sin\alpha$
or $\mathrm{M}(G)$: $Sa\cos\alpha+Fa\cos\alpha+2Mg\times0.5a\sin\alpha=Ra\sin\alpha$
Possible resolution equations:
$(\rightarrow)$: $F=S$
or $R\cos\alpha+F\sin\alpha=S\sin\alpha+(2Mg+Mg)\cos\alpha$
or $R\sin\alpha+S\cos\alpha=(2Mg+Mg)\sin\alpha+F\cos\alpha$
A1*: $S=Mg\tan\alpha$*
Official notes (completeness pass):
- N.B. Allow consistent use of a different letter for the angle in the working but must be $\alpha$ in the final answer. BOD if their $a$'s and $\alpha$'s look the same.
- M1: M(A): Correct no. of terms, dim correct, condone sin/cos confusion and sign errors. A1: Correct equation in $S$, $M$, $a$ and $\alpha$ only. N.B. Must see use of $0.5a$
- A1*: Given answer correctly obtained. (Must be in $\alpha$ but allow a different angle used in the equations). Penalise incorrect use of brackets. e.g. if they use $(90°-\alpha)$, penalise missing brackets. N.B. Must see at least one line of intermediate working which will involve : like terms collected, division by $\cos\alpha$ ,which does not need to be seen explicitly, division by 2 in some order. N.B. Allow the order of the terms on the RHS to be different and allow $m$ for $M$.
- OR M1: M(B) or M(C) or M(G) and a resolution and elimination of $F$ and $R$. Both equations used must have correct no. of terms, dim correct, condone sin/cos confusion and sign errors. A1: Correct equation in $S$, $M$, $a$ and $\alpha$ only. A1*: Given answer correctly obtained. N.B. Must see at least one line of intermediate working which will involve : like terms collected and division by $\cos\alpha$

parts.label: c
parts.text:
In a refined model
• the vertical wall is modelled as being rough
• the magnitude of the normal reaction of the ground on the rod at $A$ is $R_1$
(c) State which is greater, $R$ or $R_1$, giving a reason for your answer. (1)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) B1: The friction force at $B$ will provide an extra upward (not just vertical) force so $R_1$ will be less i.e. $R$ will be greater.
$R$ (is greater than $R_1$) as the friction act against the weight of the rod.
$R$ (is greater) as the friction acts in the same direction as $R_1$
$R$ (is greater) as the friction holds the rod up as well.
$R=3Mg=R_1+F$ so $R$ will be greater
N.B. Allow $R_1$ will be smaller with a correct reason.
B0 $R$ is greater as there is no friction from the wall.
Official notes (completeness pass):
- B1: Correct explanation. B0 if any incorrect extras

parts.text:
A second particle of mass $3M$ is now attached to the rod at $B$.
The rod again rests with end $A$ on rough horizontal ground and end $B$ against the vertical wall.
The rod lies in a vertical plane which is perpendicular to the wall.
The rod is now in limiting equilibrium at an angle $\beta$ to the wall, as shown in Figure 5.
The vertical wall is again modelled as being smooth.
The coefficient of friction between the rod and the ground is $\mu$
Given that $\tan\beta=\frac{1}{2}$
(d) use the model to show that $\mu=\frac{1}{3}$ (6)
parts.mark_scheme:
(d) EITHER: Moments about $B$ or $D$, the intersection of the normals
M1: $\mathrm{M}(B)$: $N\times2a\sin\beta=Mga\sin\beta+2Mg\times1.5a\sin\beta+F_1\times2a\cos\beta$
or $\mathrm{M}(D)$: $F_1\times2a\cos\beta=Mga\sin\beta+2Mg\times0.5a\sin\beta+3Mg\times2a\sin\beta$
A1: as above
B1: and resolve vertically: $(\uparrow)\ N=Mg+2Mg+3Mg$
OR: Moments about $A$ or $C$ or $G$
M1: A correct moments equation.
A1: A correct resolution (N.B. treat as a B mark so M0A0A1 is a possible score)
B1: A correct second resolution or a correct second moments equation
Possible Moments equations:
$\mathrm{M}(A)$: $2Mg\times0.5a\sin\beta+Mga\sin\beta+3Mg\times2a\sin\beta=P\times2a\cos\beta$
(You may see the first 2 terms collected as a single term)
or $\mathrm{M}(C)$: $0.5aF_1\cos\beta+1.5Pa\cos\beta=0.5Na\sin\beta+0.5Mga\sin\beta+3Mg\times1.5a\sin\beta$
or $\mathrm{M}(G)$: $F_1a\cos\beta+Pa\cos\beta+2Mg\times0.5a\sin\beta=Na\sin\beta+3Mga\sin\beta$
Possible resolution equations:
$(\uparrow)$: $N=Mg+2Mg+3Mg$
$(\rightarrow)$: $F_1=P$ (or $P=\mu N$)
$(\nearrow)$: $F_1\sin\beta+N\cos\beta=P\sin\beta+(3Mg+Mg+2Mg)\cos\beta$
$(\searrow)$: $N\sin\beta+P\cos\beta=(3Mg+Mg+2Mg)\sin\beta+F_1\cos\beta$
(N.B. $F_1=P=2Mg$)
dM1: Use of $F_1=\mu N$, their equations (which must be correct) and $\tan\beta=\frac{1}{2}$, to obtain an equation in $\mu$ only. N.B. This mark is only available if the previous 4 marks have all been earned.
A1*: $\mu=\frac{1}{3}$*

- EITHER M1: M(B) or M(D): Correct no. of terms, dim correct, condone sin/cos confusion and sign errors, allow use of a different letter, $\theta$ say, for $\beta$. ($\theta$ could even be $\alpha$) N.B. Condone consistent missing $a$'s. N.B. M0 if they are clearly using $R$ from part (a) for $N$.
- A1: Correct equation with at most one error. A1: Correct equation. B1: Correct vertical resolution
- OR M1: M(A or C or G): Correct no. of terms, dim correct, condone sin/cos confusion and sign errors, allow use of a different letter, $\theta$ say, for $\beta$. ($\theta$ could even be $\alpha$) N.B. Condone consistent missing $a$'s. N.B. M0 if they are clearly using $S$ from part (b) for $P$
- A1: Correct equation. A1: This is treated as a B mark for a correct resolution, seen or implied. B1: For another correct resolution or another correct moments equation (NOT about $B$) seen or implied. N.B. when entering marks on ePEN for the two resolutions, if only ONE is correct enter as A1 B0.
- dM1: Dependent for using $F_1=\mu N$ and their correct equations, to produce an equation in $\mu$ only. N.B. Allow if they use $F_1\leqslant\mu N$. A1*: Given answer correctly obtained
